The paper presents a comprehensive forced response analysis of the Pratt and Whitney Rocketdyne J-2X engine turbopumps.
A 360-degree computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis is used to capture the complex, non-cyclically symmetric dynamic pressure loading in the turbine flow field.
The temporal frequency content of the dynamic pressure from the CFD analysis provides indicators of forcing function excitation frequencies, such as multiples of blade pass frequency.
Campbell diagrams are generated using the forcing function frequencies and NASTRAN modal analysis results to identify components with modes in the engine operating range.
Cyclically symmetric structural models have been used in the past to analyze turbine vane and blade rows, but this approach does not capture the non-cyclically symmetric dynamic pressure loading.
A MATLAB script is used to calculate displacements due to the complex, cyclically asymmetric dynamic pressure components predicted by the CFD analysis.
The MATLAB-calculated displacements are read into NASTRAN, where dynamic stresses are calculated, including an adjustment for possible mistuning.
A NASTRAN static analysis is performed to calculate static stresses due to centrifugal, thermal, and pressure loading at the mode running speed.
The MATLAB script is used to generate the high cycle fatigue safety factors at each grid in the blade/vane row.

The current approach, which accounts for the non-cyclically symmetric dynamic pressure loading, provides better assurance that the worst-case safety factor has been identified compared to an approach that assumes cyclic symmetry.
The paper provides an extended example for a J-2X turbopump component.
The study focuses on the analysis of turbine vane and blade rows in the J-2X engine turbopumps.
The 360-degree CFD analysis is used to capture dynamic pressure waves caused by adjacent and non-adjacent blade/vane rows upstream and downstream of the row analyzed.
The MATLAB script is used to generate the HCFSF (high cycle fatigue safety factor) at each grid in the blade/vane row.
The paper states that forced response and static analyses are required for the prediction of combined stress and high cycle fatigue safety factors.
